description: clusterize(machines, zoom, cellPx) groups machines into a square grid measured in screen pixels, so the same cellPx covers a smaller piece of the world at every step of zoom. Projection is Web Mercator (EPSG:3857) over a 256 px tile — Leaflet's default CRS — because the grid has to line up with what is actually drawn. One entry per occupied cell: its key, the cell's column and row (cellX/cellY, which a renderer needs to keep a drawn bubble inside its own cell so two bubbles cannot overlap), how many machines fell in it, their arithmetic-mean position, and the machines themselves in the order they were given. A cell holding a single machine still comes back as a group (count 1); the caller draws those as ordinary pins, so a lone machine never becomes a bubble reading '1'. Groups are returned sorted by key, which makes the output deterministic for a given input — the order is lexicographic on the key string 'zoom:cellX:cellY' and carries no geographic meaning. Cell keys are asserted here so a Swift/Kotlin port lands on the same grid rather than a half-cell-offset one; centroids are plain arithmetic and exact, not trig, so they are compared exactly.

clusterizeCases.description: Nothing to group. An empty map is empty, not a group of zero.

A single machine still comes back as a group, with count 1 and its own position. This is what lets the caller draw it as a normal status pin instead of a bubble saying '1' — a machine on its own out in the country keeps telling you whether it works.
Two machines about 80 m apart. At zoom 10 a 64 px cell is several kilometres wide, so they share one cell and the group counts both. Its position is their midpoint.

The same two machines at zoom 18, where a 64 px cell is about 30 m across. They no longer share a cell, so they come back as two groups of one — the zoom dependence is the whole point: grouping must dissolve into individual machines as you go in.
Same pair, same zoom 18, but a 512 px cell — proof cellPx is honoured and not a constant baked into the projection.

Three machines in Lisbon and one in Porto at zoom 10: one group of three and one group of one. Order is by key, which puts the Lisbon cell first here — lexicographic, not geographic. The centroid is the mean of all three Lisbon positions, not of the cell.

Lisbon and Porto at zoom 6, where a 64 px cell is over 100 km wide — still two cells, because 275 km apart is 275 km apart. Here the key order puts Porto first: further north is a smaller cellY, and '95' sorts before '98'.

The same four machines as 'groups-and-singles-coexist', shuffled. The same cells come back in the same order, because the order is the sorted key — only the machines inside a group follow the order they were given. A caller reconciling markers against this list can rely on it not jumping around between draws.
